title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter VI
paragraphs:
My lady’s tongue is like the meadow blades,
That cut you stroking them with idle hand.
Nice cutting is her function: she divides
With spiritual edge the millet-seed,
And makes intangible savings.

As Mr. Casaubon’s carriage passed through the gateway, it blocked a small pony carriage driven by a lady with a servant behind her. Whether they recognized each other was uncertain: Mr. Casaubon gazed absently ahead, but the sharp-eyed lady managed a nod and a “How do you do?” just in time. Despite her shabby bonnet and very old Indian shawl, the deep curtsy with which the lodge keeper greeted the little carriage made clear that its occupant mattered.
“Well, Mrs. Fitchett, how are your hens laying these days?” asked the dark-eyed lady with the high colour, each word as sharply defined as carving.
“They lay well enough, ma’am, but they’ve taken to eating their eggs. I get no peace of mind with them at all.”
“Oh, the cannibals! Best sell them cheap at once. What would you take for a pair? One can’t pay high prices to eat hens with bad characters.”
“Well, ma’am, half a crown. I couldn’t let them go for less.”

“Half a crown, in these times! Come now—they’re for the Rector’s chicken broth on Sundays. He’s eaten all of ours I can spare. Remember, Mrs. Fitchett, the sermon is half your payment. Take a pair of tumbler pigeons instead—little beauties. You must come and look at them. You haven’t any tumblers among your pigeons.”
“Well, ma’am, Master Fitchett can come after work and look them over. He’s keen on new breeds; he’ll do it to oblige you.”
“Oblige me! It’ll be the best bargain he ever made. A pair of church pigeons for two wicked Spanish hens that eat their own eggs! Just don’t you and Fitchett boast too much, that’s all!”

With these last words the carriage moved on, leaving Mrs. Fitchett laughing and slowly shaking her head, punctuating it with “Sure_ly_, sure_ly_!” One might infer that she would have found the countryside duller had the Rector’s wife been less outspoken and less miserly. Indeed, farmers and labourers alike in Freshitt and Tipton would have been sadly short of conversation without stories of Mrs. Cadwallader’s sayings and doings. Here was a lady of immeasurably lofty birth, descended, as it were, from earls unknown and dim as a crowd of heroic ghosts, who pleaded poverty, beat down prices and made jokes with perfect friendliness, yet a turn of speech that reminded you who she was. Such a woman made both rank and religion seem neighbourly, softening the bitterness of tithes still paid in kind. A far more exemplary person tinged with sour dignity would not have improved anyone’s understanding of the Thirty-nine Articles, and would have done less to bind society together.
Mr. Brooke, who experienced Mrs. Cadwallader’s virtues from another angle, winced a little when her name was announced in the library, where he sat alone.

“I see you’ve had our Lowick Cicero visiting,” she said, settling comfortably into a chair and throwing back her wraps to reveal a thin but well-proportioned figure. “I suspect the two of you are cooking up bad politics, or you wouldn’t see so much of that lively gentleman. I shall report you. Remember, you’re both suspect since you supported Peel over the Catholic Bill. I’ll tell everyone you intend to stand for Middlemarch as a Whig when old Pinkerton resigns, and Casaubon will secretly help you: bribe the voters with pamphlets and open the public houses to hand them out. Come on, confess!”

“Nothing of the kind,” Mr. Brooke said, smiling and polishing his glasses, though the accusation really made him blush a little. “Casaubon and I hardly discuss politics. He doesn’t much care about philanthropy—punishments and so on. Only Church questions interest him. Not my sphere of action, you know.”

“Ra-a-ther too much your sphere, my friend. I’ve heard what you’ve been up to. Who sold a piece of land to the Papists in Middlemarch? I believe you bought it for that purpose. You’re a regular Guy Faux. See if they don’t burn you in effigy this coming fifth of November. Humphrey wouldn’t come and quarrel with you over it, so I’ve come myself.”
“Very well. I was ready to be persecuted for refusing to persecute—not persecuting, you know.”

“There you are! You’ve prepared that bit of claptrap for the election platform. Now _don’t_ let them lure you onto the platform, my dear Mr. Brooke. A man always makes a fool of himself giving speeches. His only excuse is being on the right side, so he can ask a blessing on his hemming and hawing. You’ll lose your way, I warn you. You’ll make a Saturday leftovers pie of every party’s opinions, and they’ll all pelt you.”

“That’s what I expect, you know,” Mr. Brooke said, unwilling to reveal how little he enjoyed this prophecy. “What I expect as an independent man. As for the Whigs, someone who follows the thinkers is unlikely to let any party hook him. He may go along with them up to a point—up to a certain point, you know. But that’s what you ladies never understand.”

“Where your certain point is? No, indeed. I’d like someone to explain how a man without a party can have any fixed point, roaming about and never telling his friends his address. ‘Nobody knows where Brooke will be; you can’t count on Brooke’—that’s what people say about you, to be frank. Now, do become respectable. How will you enjoy going to the Sessions with everyone avoiding your eye, a bad conscience and an empty pocket?”

“I don’t attempt to argue politics with a lady,” Mr. Brooke said with smiling unconcern, though he felt uncomfortably aware that this attack began the defensive campaign his rash actions had invited. “Your sex aren’t thinkers, you know—_varium et mutabile semper_—that kind of thing. You don’t know Virgil. I knew”—he remembered just in time that he had not personally met the Augustan poet—“I was going to say poor Stoddart, you know. That’s what _he_ said. You ladies always oppose independence, a man caring only for truth and so on. And nowhere in the county are opinions narrower than here. I don’t mean to throw stones, you know, but someone must take an independent line. If I don’t, who will?”

“Who? Any upstart without family or position. People of standing should consume their independent nonsense at home, not hawk it round. And you, about to marry your niece, as good as your daughter, to one of our best men! Sir James would be terribly annoyed. It would be too hard on him if you turned yourself into a Whig signboard now.”

Again Mr. Brooke winced inwardly. The moment Dorothea’s engagement was settled he had foreseen Mrs. Cadwallader’s taunts. An ignorant observer might easily say, “Quarrel with Mrs. Cadwallader.” But where can a country gentleman go if he quarrels with his oldest neighbours? Who could appreciate the delicate flavour of the name Brooke if it were offered casually, like wine without a seal? Certainly a man can be cosmopolitan only up to a point.
“I hope Chettam and I will always be friends, but I’m sorry to say there’s no prospect of his marrying my niece,” Mr. Brooke said, relieved to see through the window that Celia was coming in.
“Why ever not?” Mrs. Cadwallader asked, her voice sharp with surprise. “It can scarcely be two weeks since you and I were discussing it.”

“My niece has chosen another suitor—chosen him herself, you know. I had nothing to do with it. I’d have preferred Chettam; I’d have said any girl would choose him. But there’s no accounting for these matters. Your sex is changeable, you know.”
“Why, who on earth are you saying you intend to let her marry?” Mrs. Cadwallader’s mind raced through all the possible choices open to Dorothea.

But Celia now entered, glowing from her garden walk, and the greetings spared Mr. Brooke an immediate reply. He stood hurriedly, said, “By the way, I must speak to Wright about the horses,” and shuffled quickly out.
“My dear child, what’s all this about your sister being engaged?” Mrs. Cadwallader asked.
“She’s engaged to Mr. Casaubon,” Celia replied, using her usual simplest statement of fact and welcoming this chance to speak alone with the Rector’s wife.
“How frightful. How long has this been going on?”
“I only found out yesterday. The wedding is in six weeks.”
“Well, my dear, I wish you happiness in your brother-in-law.”
“I feel so sorry for Dorothea.”
“Sorry! Her own doing, I presume.”
“Yes. She says Mr. Casaubon possesses a great soul.”
“He’s welcome to it.”
“Oh, Mrs. Cadwallader, I can’t think it would be pleasant to marry a man with a great soul.”
“Well, my dear, let that be a warning. You know what one looks like now. When the next one asks to marry you, don’t accept.”
“I’m quite certain I never would.”
“No, one in a family is plenty. So your sister never cared for Sir James Chettam? How would you have liked _him_ as a brother-in-law?”
“Very much. I’m sure he’d have made a good husband. Only,” Celia added with a faint blush—sometimes she seemed to blush as naturally as she breathed—“I don’t think he’d have suited Dorothea.”
“Not lofty enough for her?”
“Dodo is terribly strict. She thinks so much about everything, and takes such care over what one says. Sir James never seemed able to please her.”
“I’m certain she must have encouraged him. That’s not much to her credit.”
“Please don’t be cross with Dodo. She doesn’t notice things. She thought so much about the cottages, and sometimes she was rude to Sir James, but he’s so kind he never took any notice.”

“Well,” Mrs. Cadwallader said, putting on her shawl and rising with apparent urgency, “I must go straight to Sir James and break the news. He’ll have brought his mother home by now, and I must call. Your uncle will never tell him. We’re all disappointed, my dear. Young people ought to consider their families when they marry. I set a bad example myself: married a poor clergyman and became an object of pity among the De Bracys, forced to scheme for my coal and pray to heaven for salad oil. Still, Casaubon has plenty of money; I’ll grant him that. As for his blood, I suppose his family arms are three black cuttlefish and a commentator rampant. By the way, before I leave I must speak to your Mrs. Carter about pastry. I want my young cook to learn from her. Poor people with four children, like us, can’t afford a good cook, you know. I’m sure Mrs. Carter will oblige me. Sir James’s cook is an absolute dragon.”
Within the hour Mrs. Cadwallader had outmanoeuvred Mrs. Carter and driven to Freshitt Hall, near her own parsonage. Her husband lived at Freshitt and employed a curate at Tipton.

Sir James Chettam had returned from the short journey that had kept him away for two days. He had changed his clothes and meant to ride to Tipton Grange. His horse waited at the door as Mrs. Cadwallader arrived, and he immediately came out, whip in hand. Lady Chettam was not back yet, but Mrs. Cadwallader could not deliver her message before the grooms. She asked him to show her the new plants in the nearby conservatory. Once they had stopped to contemplate them, she said—
“I have a tremendous shock for you. I hope you’re not as deeply in love as you claimed.”
There was no point objecting to Mrs. Cadwallader’s way of expressing herself. Still, Sir James’s face altered slightly. A vague alarm seized him.

“I do believe Brooke means to expose himself after all. I accused him of planning to stand for Middlemarch as a Liberal, and he looked foolish and never denied it. Talked about an independent line and the usual nonsense.”
“Is that everything?” Sir James asked with considerable relief.
“Why,” Mrs. Cadwallader retorted more sharply, “surely you wouldn’t want him to become a public man in that fashion, turning himself into a kind of political Cheap Jack?”
“I imagine someone could talk him out of it. He wouldn’t care for the expense.”

“That’s what I told him. Reason can reach him there. There’s always a grain or two of common sense in an ounce of stinginess. An excellent family trait, stinginess; it’s the safe direction for madness to lean. And there must be a little crack in the Brooke family, or we wouldn’t be seeing what we’re about to see.”
“What, Brooke running for Middlemarch?”

“Something worse. I feel a little responsible, really. I always told you what a fine match Miss Brooke would make. I knew she had plenty of nonsense in her, a flighty sort of Methodist stuff. But girls grow out of these things. This time, though, I’ve been caught by surprise.”

“What do you mean, Mrs. Cadwallader?” Sir James asked. He feared Miss Brooke might have run away to join the Moravian Brethren or some ridiculous sect unknown in good society. The knowledge that Mrs. Cadwallader always made the worst of things partly reassured him. “What’s happened to Miss Brooke? Please tell me plainly.”

“Very well. She’s engaged.” Mrs. Cadwallader paused, watching the deep hurt on his face as he tried to conceal it with a nervous smile and tapped his boot with his whip. Soon she added, “To Casaubon.”
Sir James dropped his whip and bent to retrieve it. Perhaps his face had never concentrated so much disgust as when he turned back to her and repeated, “Casaubon?”
“Exactly. Now you know why I came.”
“Good God! How horrible! He’s nothing but a mummy!” (Allowance must be made for the perspective of a flourishing but disappointed rival.)
“She says he’s a great soul. A great bladder full of rattling dried peas!” Mrs. Cadwallader said.
“What right has an old bachelor like that to marry?” Sir James demanded. “He’s already got one foot in the grave.”
“I suppose he intends to pull it back out.”
“Brooke shouldn’t permit it. He ought to insist they wait until she comes of age. By then she’d think better of it. What else is a guardian for?”
“As though anyone could squeeze a firm decision out of Brooke!”
“Perhaps Cadwallader could speak to him.”

“Not him! Humphrey thinks everyone’s delightful. I can never make him criticize Casaubon. He even speaks well of the bishop, though I tell him that’s unnatural in a clergyman with a benefice. What can you do with a husband who so neglects propriety? I conceal it as best I can by criticizing everyone myself. Come, come, cheer up! You’re well rid of Miss Brooke, a girl who’d expect you to see stars in daylight. Between ourselves, little Celia is worth two of her, and will probably be the better match after all. Marrying Casaubon is as good as entering a convent.”
“Oh, as for me—it’s for Miss Brooke’s sake that I think her friends ought to use their influence.”

“Well, Humphrey doesn’t know yet. But when I tell him, depend on it, he’ll say, ‘Why not? Casaubon’s a good fellow—and young—young enough.’ These charitable people can’t tell vinegar from wine until they’ve swallowed it and got colic. Still, if I were a man I’d prefer Celia, particularly once Dorothea had gone. The truth is, you’ve courted one and won the other. I can see she admires you almost as much as a man expects to be admired. From anyone but me you might think that an exaggeration. Goodbye!”

Sir James helped Mrs. Cadwallader into her carriage and then mounted his horse. His friend’s unpleasant news would not deprive him of his ride. He would simply ride faster, in a direction away from Tipton Grange.

Now, why on earth should Mrs. Cadwallader concern herself with Miss Brooke’s marriage? Why, once the match she liked to think she had helped arrange fell through, did she immediately lay the groundwork for another? Was there some clever plot, some furtive course of action a careful watcher with a telescope could uncover? Not at all. A telescope could have swept Tipton and Freshitt, the whole territory of her pony carriage, without detecting a suspicious meeting or any scene from which she returned with less than her usual undisturbed sharpness of eye and naturally high colour. Had that convenient vehicle existed in the time of the Seven Sages, one of them would surely have observed that following women in their pony carriages teaches you little about them. Even when we point a microscope at a drop of water, our interpretations turn out rather crude. Through a weak lens we may seem to see a creature displaying energetic greed as smaller creatures swim into it like so many animated tax pennies. A stronger lens reveals tiny hairs creating whirlpools for these victims, while the swallower waits passively at its tax office. In the same metaphorical way, a strong lens applied to Mrs. Cadwallader’s matchmaking reveals minute causes at work, creating what we might call whirlpools of thought and speech that deliver the nourishment she needs. Her life had a simple country character, free from secrets foul, dangerous or otherwise important, and consciously untouched by the world’s great affairs. Affairs in the great world therefore interested her all the more when letters from aristocratic relatives brought them: how fascinating younger sons had ruined themselves by marrying their mistresses; young Lord Tapir’s fine, blue-blooded idiocy; old Lord Megatherium’s furious, gouty tempers; the precise intersection of family trees that had carried a coronet to a fresh branch and extended scandal’s connections. She retained every detail with complete accuracy and served them in an excellent pickle of epigrams. These pleased her the more because she believed in good birth and its absence as unquestioningly as in game and vermin. Poverty would never have made her disown anyone. A De Bracy reduced to eating dinner from a basin would have seemed a touching spectacle worth embellishing, and I fear his aristocratic vices would not have horrified her. Her feeling for the vulgar rich, however, approached religious hatred. They had probably made their money through high retail prices, and she hated high prices for anything not supplied to the Rectory as payment in kind. Such people had no place in God’s design for the world, and their accents tormented the ears. A town full of these monsters was little more than low comedy, unworthy of inclusion in a well-bred scheme of the universe. Any lady tempted to judge Mrs. Cadwallader harshly should examine how comprehensive her own beautiful views are, and make quite sure they have room for every life honoured with existence alongside her own.

With a mind as active as phosphorus, biting everything nearby into its preferred shape, how could Mrs. Cadwallader consider the Miss Brookes and their marriage prospects no concern of hers? Especially when she had spent years scolding Mr. Brooke with friendly frankness and confidentially informing him that she thought him a poor creature. From the girls’ arrival in Tipton she had arranged in advance Dorothea’s marriage to Sir James. Had it happened, she would have been quite sure she had caused it. Its failure to happen after she had conceived it provoked an irritation every thinker can understand. She was the diplomat of Tipton and Freshitt, and anything happening against her plans was an offensive breach of order. She had no patience with whims like Miss Brooke’s. She now realized that some of her husband’s weak charitableness had infected her judgment of the girl: those Methodist fancies, that air of being more religious than rector and curate combined, came from a deeper, more ingrained disease than she had cared to believe.

“Still,” Mrs. Cadwallader told herself first and her husband later, “I wash my hands of her. If she’d married Sir James, she might have become a sane, sensible woman. He’d never have contradicted her, and without contradiction a woman has no reason to cling stubbornly to her absurdities. But now I wish her joy of her hair shirt.”

Naturally Mrs. Cadwallader had to choose another match for Sir James. Once she had made up her mind that it should be the younger Miss Brooke, she could scarcely have made a shrewder move towards her plan’s success than hinting to the baronet that he had touched Celia’s heart. He was not one of those gentlemen who pine after Sappho’s unreachable apple, laughing on the highest branch—those charms that

“Smile like a clump of cowslips on a cliff,
Beyond the reach of any willing hand.”

He had no sonnets to write, and could take no pleasure in discovering that the woman he preferred did not prefer him. The knowledge that Dorothea had chosen Mr. Casaubon had already bruised his attachment and loosened its grip. A sportsman he might be, but he felt differently about women than about grouse and foxes. He did not view his future wife as prey valued mainly for the excitement of pursuit. Nor was he so familiar with the customs of primitive peoples that he felt some symbolic combat for her, tomahawk in hand, necessary to preserve the historical continuity of marriage. Instead, he possessed the amiable vanity that draws us to people who like us and away from those who do not, along with a grateful, good nature. Merely imagining a woman’s kindness towards him spun little threads of tenderness from his heart to hers.

So, after riding quite fast away from Tipton Grange for half an hour, Sir James slowed down and eventually turned onto a road offering a shorter route back. Various feelings combined to make him decide to visit the Grange that day after all, as though nothing had changed. He could not help feeling glad he had never proposed and been rejected. Ordinary friendly courtesy required him to call about the cottages; fortunately Mrs. Cadwallader had now prepared him to offer congratulations, if necessary, without excessive awkwardness. He truly disliked it: giving Dorothea up hurt badly. Yet deciding to make the visit immediately and master every outward sign of emotion offered a kind of teeth-gritting resistance, one irritation countering another. And although he did not clearly recognize the impulse, he certainly knew Celia would be there, and that he would pay her more attention than before.

We mortals, women and men alike, swallow plenty of disappointments between breakfast and dinner. We hold back tears, grow a little pale around the lips and answer questions with “Oh, nothing!” Pride helps us, and pride is no bad thing when it merely prompts us to hide our own wounds rather than wound other people.
